title: Satheesan’s Kerala: A 21-Member Cabinet, a Broke Treasury, and a Diaspora Watching Every Move
excerpt: The UDF’s return to power after a decade in opposition is being felt from Thiruvananthapuram to Dubai. With 3.5 million Keralites abroad, the new government’s first hundred days will be judged as much in Gulf living rooms as in the Kerala Assembly.
body:
The last time the United Democratic Front ran Kerala, the Gulf boom was still cushioning every household budget in Thrissur and Malappuram. A decade later, V.D. Satheesan walks into the Chief Minister’s office on May 18 inheriting a state treasury that has been scraped clean — and a diaspora that is no longer content to simply wire money home and stay quiet.

## A Full-Cabinet Gamble

Satheesan’s decision to swear in all 21 ministers on the same day is a deliberate break from Kerala’s tradition of staggered oath ceremonies. The 20-member cabinet — 11 Congress berths, five for the Indian Union Muslim League, and the rest distributed among smaller alliance partners — includes three women, two Scheduled Caste members, and, most notably, Ramesh Chennithala, the man who wanted the top job himself.

The Congress-led UDF swept 102 of 140 assembly seats in the April elections, ending the Left Democratic Front’s decade-long hold on power. Satheesan, a 25-year legislative veteran from Paravur, ran a methodical campaign that stayed relentlessly on message: governance, fiscal discipline, and jobs. Senior leaders including AICC president Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi are expected at the Central Stadium ceremony in Thiruvananthapuram, alongside chief ministers from Karnataka, Telangana, and Himachal Pradesh. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay’s presence is also confirmed — a gesture that underscores the broader Congress realignment across southern India.

## The Gulf Factor

The numbers tell the story. Kerala’s Gulf diaspora — estimated at 3.5 million, the largest from any single Indian state — sends home remittances that have historically accounted for over a third of the state’s GDP. But that lifeline is fraying. Saudization policies, automation in the UAE construction sector, and a generational shift among younger Keralites who prefer tech jobs in Bengaluru or Toronto over contract work in Sharjah have all eroded the traditional migration pipeline.

The LDF government’s handling of Gulf returnees during and after the pandemic drew sharp criticism from NRI associations. Over 500,000 workers returned to Kerala between 2020 and 2022, many with depleted savings and no reintegration plan. Satheesan has promised a dedicated NRI rehabilitation ministry — a pledge that Gulf-based Keralite associations have publicly said they will hold him to within his first hundred days.

## Fiscal Tightrope

Kerala’s debt-to-GDP ratio has ballooned past 37 per cent, among the highest of any Indian state. Satheesan’s first signal has been conspicuously austere: he announced he would use his existing official car rather than procure a new one, urged ministers to reduce convoy sizes, and called for a freeze on luxury spending. These are optics, but they are optics calibrated for a state where public anger over fiscal mismanagement helped topple a sitting government.

The real test will be the budget session. Kerala’s social welfare commitments — pensions, healthcare, education subsidies — are sacrosanct in a state with India’s highest Human Development Index. Satheesan’s challenge is to fund them without the Gulf remittance surplus that previous UDF governments took for granted.

## What the Diaspora Is Watching

In WhatsApp groups from Abu Dhabi to Edison, New Jersey, the conversation is not about Satheesan’s ideology — it is about property tax reform, NORKA-ROOTS efficiency, and whether the new government will actually digitise land records. Kerala’s NRIs own a disproportionate share of the state’s real estate, and every change in property regulations is felt in household budgets across three continents.

For the 800,000-odd Keralites in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, the UDF’s return also carries a cultural signal. Kerala’s Communist governments were associated with muscular trade unionism and scepticism toward private enterprise. Satheesan’s Congress promises a friendlier climate for investment, startup incubation, and IT corridors — the kind of economy that second-generation NRIs might actually consider returning to.

The swearing-in is tomorrow. The real governance starts the day after. And three and a half million people who left Kerala but never stopped calling it home will be watching.
